title: Python generators: values on demand

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own lesson text and examples on python generators: values on demand, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can write a generator with yield and predict when its code runs
can chain generators into a pipeline that never holds all the data
can choose between a list comprehension and a generator expression

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: Reading a 2 GB log file into a list crashes a small server; reading it line by line with a generator uses a few kilobytes. Generators are how Python handles data that is large, endless or expensive to produce, and they are behind `range`, file reading, `zip` and `map`. Interviewers ask about them to see whether you understand **when code actually runs**.

sections.heading: yield pauses a function
sections.body:
A function containing `yield` is a **generator function**. Calling it does **not run its body**: it returns a generator object, paused before the first line.

Each `next(gen)` resumes the body until the next `yield`, hands back that value, and pauses again, **keeping all local variables**. When the body ends, the generator raises `StopIteration`, which a `for` loop treats as "done".

So a generator produces values **one at a time, only when asked**. This is called **lazy evaluation**. Memory use stays constant no matter how many values it produces, because only the current state is kept.

> **Note:** A generator can be consumed **only once**. After the loop finishes, iterating again gives nothing. If you need the values twice, store them in a list, or call the generator function again to get a fresh generator.

sections.heading: When does the code run?
sections.body: The prints inside the generator show exactly when its body runs: not when it is created, but as `next` and the `for` loop ask for values.

code.src:
def tokens(start, count):
    print("  (generator starts)")
    for n in range(start, start + count):
        print(f"  (making token {n})")
        yield f"T{n}"
    print("  (generator finished)")

gen = tokens(101, 3)
print("created, nothing has run yet")
print("first:", next(gen))
for t in gen:                       # the loop calls next() until StopIteration
    print("loop got", t)
code.expected_output:
created, nothing has run yet
  (generator starts)
  (making token 101)
first: T101
  (making token 102)
loop got T102
  (making token 103)
loop got T103
  (generator finished)
code.caption: A generator runs only when asked for the next value

sections.heading: Pipelines and generator expressions
sections.body:
Generators **compose**. One generator can consume another, so you can build a pipeline: read lines → skip comments → convert → accumulate. Each stage pulls one item from the stage before it, does its work, and passes one item on. At no point does any stage hold the whole data set.

A **generator expression** is the lazy cousin of a list comprehension: `(n * n for n in nums)` with round brackets instead of square ones. Pass it straight into a function that consumes an iterable: `sum(n * n for n in range(10**6))` adds a million squares without building a million-item list.

| Use | When |
|---|---|
| list comprehension `[...]` | you need the values more than once, need `len`, indexing or sorting |
| generator expression `(...)` | you consume the values once, especially into `sum`, `max`, `any`, `join` |

sections.heading: A small pipeline
sections.body: `readings` cleans raw lines, `running_total` accumulates them, and neither knows about the other. The last line compares the size of a list of 100,000 numbers with a generator over the same numbers.

code.src:
import sys

def readings(lines):
    for line in lines:                  # one line at a time, never the whole file
        line = line.strip()
        if line and not line.startswith("#"):
            yield int(line)

def running_total(values):
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total += v
        yield total

orders = ["120", "# lunch rush", "80", "", "200"]
print(list(running_total(readings(orders))))
squares = sum(n * n for n in range(1, 1_000_001))   # no million-item list is built
print(squares)
print(sys.getsizeof([n for n in range(10**5)]) > 100_000, sys.getsizeof(n for n in range(10**5)) < 1_000)
code.caption: A pipeline of generators, and a generator expression

sections.heading: Generators in real code
sections.body:
Some places you will meet them:

- **Files.** `for line in open(path):` already reads lazily, one line at a time. Wrapping it in a generator that parses and filters keeps the whole program streaming.
- **Paginated APIs.** A generator can fetch page 1, yield its items, fetch page 2 only when the caller wants more, and stop when the server says there are no more pages. The caller just writes a `for` loop.
- **Infinite sequences.** `itertools.count()` never ends, which is fine because nobody asks for all of it; `itertools.islice(gen, 10)` takes the first ten.
- **`yield from other`** hands every value of another iterable through, which keeps recursive generators (walking a folder tree, say) short.

One caution: because the body runs later, errors appear later too. A generator that reads a missing file does not fail when you create it, only when the first value is requested, which can be far away in the code. Keep the place that creates a generator close to the place that consumes it.

Another caution is debugging: `print(gen)` shows only `<generator object ...>`. To see the values, convert a *small* one with `list(gen)`, remembering that this consumes it.

sections.heading: Tracing the hands-on generator
sections.body:
The task asks for `running_max(values)`, a generator that yields the best score so far after each score. Plan it with the same shape as `running_total` above: one variable of state, updated before each `yield`.

Trace it on `3 7 2 9 9`:

| value read | best before | best after | yielded |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | none yet | 3 | 3 |
| 7 | 3 | 7 | 7 |
| 2 | 7 | 7 | 7 |
| 9 | 7 | 9 | 9 |
| 9 | 9 | 9 | 9 |

The first value needs care: there is no "best so far" yet. Starting `best` at `0` would be wrong for negative scores (the running maximum of `-4` is `-4`, not `0`). Start it at `None` and take the first value as it is, or start it at `float("-inf")`.

Notice also what the main program passes in: `(int(x) for x in data[1:])`, a generator expression. Your generator consumes another generator, and the `join` at the end consumes yours. Not one list of scores is built anywhere in the pipeline.

sections.heading: Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think calling a generator function runs it.** It only creates the generator; the body starts at the first `next`.

**Many students think a generator can be reused like a list.** Once exhausted it stays empty. `list(gen)` twice gives the values and then `[]`.

**Many students think generators are always faster.** They save memory, not necessarily time. For a small collection used several times, a list is simpler and often quicker.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.q: What is the difference between return and yield?
qa.a: return ends the function and gives back one value. yield gives back a value and pauses the function with its local state intact, so the next request resumes right after the yield. A function with yield becomes a generator.

qa.q: How would you process a 10 GB file of numbers in Python?
qa.a: Iterate the file line by line, which is already lazy, and pass the lines through generators that parse and filter, consuming the result with sum or a loop. Memory stays constant because no stage holds the whole file.

A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory immediately, so it supports len, indexing and repeated iteration. A generator expression produces values lazily, once, which is ideal for feeding sum, max or any over large data.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- `yield` turns a function into a generator; calling it runs nothing yet.
- `next` resumes until the next `yield`; local state survives between values.
- Generators are single-use and memory-light.
- Chain them into pipelines; each stage pulls one item at a time.
- `(...)` generator expressions for one-pass consumption, `[...]` lists for reuse.

quiz.stem: `def g(): print('A'); yield 1`. What prints after `x = g()`?
quiz.explanation: Creating the generator runs none of its body.

quiz.stem: `gen = (n for n in range(3)); list(gen); list(gen)`. What does the second `list(gen)` return?
quiz.explanation: A generator is exhausted after one full pass.
The generator expression never builds a list.

quiz.stem: After `yield`, what happens to the generator's local variables?
options: They are kept until the next value is requested
They are copied to the caller
quiz.explanation: The generator pauses with its state intact.

hands_on.title: Best score so far
hands_on.task: Read `n`, then `n` integers (quiz scores in order). Write the generator `running_max(values)` that yields, after each score, **the highest score seen so far**. The program prints the yielded values on one line. Do not build a list inside `running_max`.
hands_on.starter:
import sys


def running_max(values):
    # Yield, after each value, the largest value seen so far.
    # TODO: your code here
    yield from values


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    values = (int(x) for x in data[1:])
    print(" ".join(str(m) for m in running_max(values)))


main()
hands_on.solution:
import sys


def running_max(values):
    best = None
    for v in values:
        best = v if best is None else max(best, v)
        yield best


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    values = (int(x) for x in data[1:])
    print(" ".join(str(m) for m in running_max(values)))


main()

revision_card.front: Generators: when does the body run, what do they save, and their limits?
revision_card.back: Body runs only on next()/iteration, pausing at each yield with state kept. Constant memory, lazy; pipelines pull one item at a time. Single use; errors show up when consumed.
